raw: {"choice":"A","rationale":"A is more balanced and decision-useful: it distinguishes browser-native libraries from full engines, covers a broader practical set of options, and gives a clear selection matrix tied to use cases and durability. Both responses contain some overgeneralizations, but B makes more questionable or overly specific claims—especially around PlayCanvas having built-in real-time multiplayer, rigid Godot mobile-web support wording, and exact size/pricing assertions—while A is generally better calibrated about trade-offs, ecosystem risk, and web-export constraints."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is better structured and more decision-useful: it cleanly distinguishes full engines from rendering libraries, covers a broader set of credible options, and its recommendation matrix maps choices to concrete project constraints. Its longevity discussion is generally more nuanced, especially around ownership and web-native alignment. B has useful additions, but contains more questionable or misleading claims—particularly about Phaser physics and PlayCanvas having no single-company dependency—and its final recommendation is less carefully qualified."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is more complete and better prioritized around structural controls: immutable agent guardrails, explicit lifecycle-script containment, append-only auditing, rollback, and clear separation of OS-enforced boundaries from model behavior. It also correctly treats model unreliability as a first-class source of equivalent blast radius. B adds a valuable cloud-provider/privacy boundary and has stronger residual-risk discussion, but its v1 command allowlist is less robust than capability confinement, its filesystem “path-prefix check” framing is overly simplistic, and deferring self-modification protection weakens the first-release posture."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is stronger overall because it more consistently treats the model as an untrusted decision-maker and prioritizes structural controls over prompt-level assurances. It identifies important practical paths A underweights, especially lifecycle-script execution and compromise of the agent’s own update channel, and explains why approval-only controls are vulnerable to fatigue. Its phased plan is more actionable around containment, immutable guardrails, auditability, rollback, and capability-based permissions. There is some overlap between its v1 confinement and v2 sandbox descriptions, but that is a minor clarity issue; A has more significant prioritization and implementation weaknesses, including deferring package provenance too far and overstating simplistic path checks as robust filesystem enforcement."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is materially clearer and more actionable: it presents one coherent procedure, explicit assumptions, sensitivity metric, allocation rule, validation checks, and failure modes. B begins with the same content but then repeats it extensively with irrelevant connective filler, severely harming structure and usability without adding insight. Both share technical limitations—especially strong claims about universal U-shaped/attention sensitivity and a sequential score that confounds marginal layer importance with ordering—but A communicates these assumptions and limitations far more effectively."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is substantially clearer and more usable: it presents the same substantive proposal once, in a coherent progression from empirical claims through assumptions, procedure, and validation. A is burdened by extensive duplicated text and intrusive connective fragments that severely damage structure and actionability. Both share important limitations—especially overgeneralizing sensitivity patterns and relying on a path-dependent sequential score despite layer interactions—but B communicates those assumptions and validation checks far more effectively."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is better structured and more appropriately calibrated about the limited inferential value of 200 runs, especially its distinction between task coverage and repeat noise and its explicit inconclusive-reporting rules. Its numerical variance assumptions and treatment of pairing are oversimplified, and CI overlap is not a valid equivalence criterion, but A has more serious internal design failures: it allocates extra repeats to ten “hard” tasks despite defining only six, misstates per-language sample sizes, and gives overly optimistic independent-proportion power claims despite repeated task structure."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is stronger because it correctly identifies tasks—not the 200 episodes—as the main source of independent evidence for language effects and explicitly avoids treating repeats as independent observations. It uses a coherent crossed design, stratifies difficulty, and gives a substantially more honest account of inconclusive pairwise comparisons with uncertainty and MDE reporting. Its numerical power calculation and pilot/rebalancing plan are somewhat overconfident and internally awkward because pilot tasks are later excluded, but B has more fundamental flaws: its power argument treats correlated repeated task runs as independent two-proportion samples, misstates per-language run counts, and includes visible arithmetic correction text that weakens clarity and pre-registration credibility."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is materially clearer and more usable because it presents the same substantive design once, with a coherent progression from triage through promotion, deduplication, and bias controls. A begins equivalently but then repeats the document several times with intrusive filler, which severely harms structure and actionability. Neither is especially well calibrated: both use unsupported fixed timing/threshold claims, conflate operational failures with model disqualification, and propose statistically weak small benchmark samples; nevertheless, B preserves the stronger parts of the shared reasoning without A’s catastrophic clarity failure."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is clearly better because it presents one coherent, navigable design, whereas B reproduces the same content repeatedly with distracting filler and severe structural corruption. Both share substantive weaknesses—overconfident timing and thresholds, overly brittle single-test disqualifications, and an internally confused predictor proposal—but A remains actionable and readable enough to assess and revise; B’s duplication materially undermines clarity and usability."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is better structured and more actionable: it maps objectives to concrete outputs, specifies usable features, defines prioritization and budget-gap decisions, includes evaluation metrics, and offers an implementation roadmap. A is still overconfident in several model choices, but provides the stronger starting design."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is better structured and more actionable while avoiding several of B’s serious implementation and framing errors. It sensibly uses expected value and time remaining for prioritization, distinguishes descriptive budget-gap scoring from optional anomaly detection, and frames lifecycle behavior as transitions rather than an ill-specified generic classifier. Both responses over-prescribe ML before establishing data quality, intervention constraints, causal measurement, and whether lost reasons are labeled; neither sufficiently addresses leakage or offline-to-business validation. But B additionally contains multiple technical inconsistencies (duplicated/noisy schema, an ill-defined budget target, fragile row-wise probability code, incorrect class-probability indexing assumptions, and a lifecycle feature/label construction that appears to drop the current stage), reducing its reliability."}

Both share limitations—overconfident cost figures, insufficient experimental controls and support-specific safety/escalation metrics—but B presents the reasoning cleanly."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A and B share the same substantive framework, but B appends large, repetitive, poorly integrated duplications with filler transitions that materially damage clarity and actionability. A is therefore clearly superior on structure and usability, though both would benefit from more calibrated cost ranges and more rigorous evaluation design."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is stronger because it starts from distinct failure modes and maps each to layered, actionable signals across request, batch/scheduler, cache, and hardware scopes. Its stall rules explicitly distinguish single-request blockage, whole-batch wedges, speculative collapse, memory pressure, and scheduler livelock, producing clearer operational triage than A’s primarily request-centric approach. B also better explains trace/log correlation and avoids paging on healthy long work through progress guards and systemic thresholds. Both have minor calibration weaknesses—especially fixed illustrative thresholds and B’s potentially overbroad cache-hit SLO—but B is more complete, structured, and diagnostically insightful."}

{"choice":"A","rationale":"A is more complete and operationally sound: it separates request, batch, scheduler, cache, speculative-decoding, hardware, and tracing signals; gives concrete failure signatures; and uses sustained absence of progress plus system context rather than duration. Its alert tiers appropriately distinguish page-worthy systemic stalls from individual pathological requests and capacity trends. B has useful cardinality and self-calibration ideas, but its heartbeat threshold can be unrealistically sensitive, and some suppression logic is questionable (for example, cache-hit ratio should chiefly affect prefill, not decode ITL)."}

{"choice":"tie","rationale":"The responses are substantively identical, with the same crossed design, task stratification, mixed-effects framing, power calculations, and explicit inconclusiveness reporting. {"choice":"tie","rationale":"The responses are textually identical, so neither is better on reasoning, depth, structure, actionability, or uncertainty calibration."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is stronger because its explicit third category, C (confounded), captures the central transfer risk: quality findings obtained under laptop-forced quantization, truncation, or serving changes are neither automatically model mechanisms nor merely hardware metrics. That framing yields a concrete re-measurement and reporting workflow, including calibration, precision/context/batching checks, tag audits, and a dedicated reconciliation section. A has useful operational detail and correctly flags rank reversals, but its initial treatment of qualitative rankings as mechanisms is too permissive and its binary M/H taxonomy is less calibrated for configuration-dependent quality claims."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is stronger because it treats transferability as conditional on preserving the effective evaluation configuration, explicitly anticipates quantization- and context-driven rank reversals, distinguishes controlled re-evaluation from an expanded candidate study, and makes reproducibility requirements concrete. B still slightly overstates that some qualitative findings inherently transfer, but its boundary-case analysis and report safeguards are materially better calibrated."}

{"choice":"B","rationale":"B is more soundly structured and comprehensive: it separates architecture-level cache reduction from runtime eviction, includes major approaches such as MQA/GQA and MLA, clearly identifies orthogonality with quantization, and gives a practical hybrid policy tied to an agent’s shifting working set. A’s code could be more complete around masking and production training details, but its omissions are less harmful than B’s concrete pitfalls."}
